question: What is the difference between `std::sort()` and `std::stable_sort()`?

scenes.sub: Both sort. Only one promises what happens to ties.
scenes.say: Sort versus stable sort. Both put your data in order. The difference is what happens to elements that compare equal.

scenes.head: Sort by grade, highest first
scenes.say: Four students, sorted by grade, highest first. Ann and Cid tie at ninety, Bob and Dan at eighty five. Stable sort guarantees that equal elements keep their original order. Ann was before Cid, so Ann stays before Cid, every time. Plain sort only promises the grades end up in order. Ties can come out in any order, like Cid before Ann. On tiny inputs you may not see it, because short ranges often use insertion sort, which happens to be stable. Don't rely on that.

scenes.head: Where stability pays off: sorting in passes
scenes.say: Where stability matters: sorting by several keys in passes, like clicking column headers in a spreadsheet. Sort by name first, then stable sort by grade. Within each grade, the names stay alphabetical, because the second pass never scrambles ties. If you can write one combined comparator instead, a single plain sort does the same job.

scenes.head: Side by side
rows: O(n log n), O(n log² n) without spare memory
Use when ties must keep their order
scenes.say: Equal elements: sort may reorder them, stable sort keeps them. Algorithms: sort is typically introsort, a quicksort that falls back to heapsort, and stable sort is typically merge sort. Time: both O of n log n, but stable sort drops to n log squared n when it can't get extra memory. Memory: sort works in place, stable sort tries to allocate a buffer. So in practice, sort is usually faster.

lines: stable_sort keeps equal elements in their original relative order. sort doesn't.
Both O(n log n). stable_sort needs a buffer, or degrades to O(n log² n).
Use stable_sort for multi-pass or multi-key sorting where ties matter.
scenes.say: Stable sort keeps equal elements in their original order. Sort makes no such promise. Both are O of n log n, but stable sort needs extra memory to get there. Use stable sort when the order of ties matters.
